newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Systems, prices seen key to Ericsson H1.
newsitem.headline: Systems, prices seen key to Ericsson H1.

text.p: Sweden's Ericsson, one of the world's closely-watched high-tech stocks, reports first half earnings on Thursday with analysts looking for better systems sales and at falling prices for ever-smaller mobile phones.

Analysts expect telecoms group AB LM Ericsson to post a pre-tax profit of 5.11 billion crowns for the first half of 1997, a 21-percent increase on the same 1996 period. The result is due by 0900 GMT on Thursday.

The share has rocketed 34 percent since it reported its first quarter earnings and analysts are keen for any signals from the company about cost cutting and the delicate balance between mobile telephone sales versus mobile infrastructure.

Few expect Ericsson to repeat a 100-percent growth figure for mobile phones and terminals which it reported for the first quarter. Most are hoping mobile systems sales growth, a wan 16 percent last quarter, will return to higher 1996 levels.
Analysts said they would be looking for a reduction in R&D spending, which totalled 14 percent of sales in 1996.
"After the first quarter people started to worry that maybe Ericsson was getting too dependent on the lower-margin handset business," Schroeder technology analyst Susan Anthony said.
"One will be looking to see sales growth in mobile phones systems," she said.
Ericsson said sales of mobile telephones and terminals accounts for about 18 percent of total sales in 1996. Sales were 30.71 billion crowns in the first quarter of the year.
Mobile systems, the group's largest division, accounted for 47 percent and Infocom Systems, or public telecoms, 32 percent.
Ericsson watchers are keen for news of cost cutting in its public telecoms unit and developments on the key Chinese market.
"The major area where there's still a lot to do is Infocom, which is why any comment on how their progress is there will be important," Anthony said.

Ulf Hellzen, a telecoms analyst at Swedbank, said the Chinese fixed exchange market was a sticky area for Canadian telecoms equipment maker Northern Telecom Ltd. (Nortel) which also posted second quarter earnings this week.
"There's a risk Ericsson will also perform quite weakly in China," Hellzen said.
Hellzen said Nortel's improved performance of its public networks operations through rationalisation was encouraging.

"They can do it, Ericsson can do it. That's the theme really for Ericsson today -- they have to cut costs," Hellzen said. Players are also looking for falling handset prices. Finnish rival Nokia Oy said in April it expected erosion of 15-20 percent on average this year.

U.S. rival Motorola Inc. has said it is dealing with falling prices by focussing on mid- and high-tier products which have higher margins. An example of this is its tiny StarTAC phone, which competes with Ericsson's GF 788 model.
Analysts said Ericsson's report would have to contain very good news for the share to rise from these levels.
"It might go up in the short-term but there's a lot of good news in the share price already. We're not really optimistic about the share price," Peter Roe, telecoms analyst at Paribas, told Reuters.
"One could argue that at these levels it's fully-valued. But in these markets, who can say? asked Morgan Stanley analyst Angela Dean.
At 1025 GMT the share was trading at 334.5 crowns, up 4.5 on the day, compared to its closing price of 249.5 crowns on April 25 when it published its first quarter figures.
